newsitem.title: TURKEY: Turkish council meets amid coalition strife.
newsitem.headline: Turkish council meets amid coalition strife.

text.p: Turkey's military-dominated National Security Council held talks on Monday in the shadow of a coalition rift caused by army demands for curbs on Islamist revivalism.
Generals and civilian leaders walked into the regular monthly meeting at President Suleyman Demirel's official residence carrying thick files and briefcases.
A call by the council a month ago to keep Islam out of public life has exposed cracks in Prime Minister Necmettin Erbakan's Islamist-led government.
A minister from the pro-Western True Path Party wing of the alliance was quoted on Monday as proposing breaking up the coalition and replacing it with a secularist team.

"This government cannot find a solution to the tension in the country. A new, broad-based government must be formed without wasting any time," the Hurriyet daily quoted Trade and Industry Minister Yalim Erez as saying.
Erez and fellow True Path Party members have become increasingly critical of what they see as Erbakan's reluctance to implement the army's demands.
The council's full agenda for Monday's meeting was not made public, but Erbakan on Sunday denied media reports that an army attempt to restrict religious education would be discussed.
Istanbul stocks jumped 4.5 percent in the morning session on hopes that the army would not pressurise Erbakan at the meeting.

The generals want to see a cut in the number of "Imam Hatip" Islamic secondary schools, enforcement of a ban on Islamic dress and an assault on pro-Islamist media and business as part of a planned return to Turkey's rigid secularism of the 1920s.
Erbakan, the first Islamist to lead NATO-member Turkey, has agreed to the demands in principle but his government has yet to expedite any of them.
Some Turkish newspapers said the fiercely secularist generals would give the government until the end of April to produce evidence it is complying.

The army has deposed three civilian leaders since 1960. A military source told Reuters the army was reluctant to move against this government despite unease at a bid by Erbakan to introduce mild Islamist reforms.

"It has been seen that military administrations don't solve anything," the source said. Analysts say the generals may try to force more True Path MPs to rebel against the coalition if Erbakan does not toe the line.
The True Path, headed by Foreign Minister Tansu Ciller, has close ties to the security establishment.
Health Minister Yildirim Aktuna, a True Path member, on Monday repeated doubts he voiced last week on the future of the alliance, Anatolian news agency said.

Erbakan has also faced a backlash from the secularist majority. Almost 10,000 people chanted "Turkey is secularist and will stay that way," at a classical music concert in Ankara attended by the president on Sunday.
"This is modern Turkey," the Hurriyet daily said in a front-page banner headline above a photograph of the concert, broadcast live on television.
